solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Force husband into faith

indicators.note: putting one thing into another means it sits inside it

blocks.note: H is the standard abbreviation for husband
faith in someone is trust in them

explanation.surface: Someone coerces their husband into adopting a religion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Faith' reads as religion, but here it means confidence in someone, and the husband's letter goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A thrust is a forceful push, so the noun is a synonym for force applied suddenly.

clue.text: Traitor’s prime motive?

definitions.note: the whole clue doubles as a cryptic description of the crime a traitor commits

indicators.note: prime means first in rank, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: the initial of the word
a motive is the reason for doing something

explanation.surface: A question about what chiefly drives someone who betrays their country.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue works twice: as wordplay it is an initial plus a synonym, and read straight it hints at the crime itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Treason is the crime of betraying one's country, which is exactly what defines a traitor and what one is driven towards.

clue.text: Storyteller near court in full flow

indicators.note: something in full flow is moving freely, so the letters pour out in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A talkative storyteller holds forth close to a law court or royal court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In full flow' describes a talker in the surface, which is why it disguises the rearranging so well.
explanation.definitionFit: A raconteur is a person skilled at telling anecdotes entertainingly, so it is a synonym for a narrator of tales.

clue.text: Succeeded tucking into Pacific state’s fried pastry

indicators.note: tucking into something means slipping inside it

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for succeeded, as in family trees
Samoa is an island nation in the South Pacific

explanation.surface: Someone has managed to eat a fried pastry from a Pacific island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tucking into' suggests eating, which suits the food in the surface, but it signals one piece going inside another.
explanation.definitionFit: A samosa is a triangular fried South Asian snack of spiced filling in a thin crisp casing.

clue.text: Brave force before noble mix-up ousting master

indicators.note: coming before means placed in front, fixing the running order
to oust is to throw out, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: F is the symbol for force in physics
an earl is a nobleman
a mix-up is a mess
M is an abbreviation for master

explanation.surface: A courageous display of power precedes an aristocratic muddle that removes the man in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: The master's letter comes out of the muddle, leaving ESS to finish the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Fearless means showing no fear at all, which is a close synonym of courageous and bold.

clue.text: Uncomfortably lean style

indicators.note: something sitting uncomfortably is out of place, so the letters shift into another order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone thin carries off an awkward, gaunt kind of fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uncomfortably lean' reads as a description of a skinny look, but the adverb is only the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Elan is flair and vigorous panache, so it matches style in the sense of distinctive dash.

clue.text: Shopkeeper retired, one to lament losing cover

indicators.note: in a down entry the cover is the top, so the word loses its uppermost letter

blocks.note: RET is the standard abbreviation for retired
someone who laments wails, so is a wailer

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper who has retired has become a mourner who has lost their protection.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'cover' is the top letter, like a lid, so the wailer loses its W.
explanation.definitionFit: A retailer sells goods directly to the public, as someone who runs a shop does.

clue.text: Starting off panic is a mistake

indicators.note: with its start taken off, the word loses its opening letter

blocks.note: panic is extreme fear, terror

explanation.surface: Setting off a panic is a bad idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starting off' reads as triggering, but it means the first letter is taken off the fear.
explanation.definitionFit: An error is a wrong act or judgement, so the two words are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: Prominent foreigner needling saint

indicators.note: a needle pierces into something, so one piece is pushed inside another

blocks.note: an alien is a foreign national
ST is the abbreviation for saint

explanation.surface: A well-known outsider is annoying a holy person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Needling' reads as irritating, but it means stitching into, so the foreigner goes inside the saint.
explanation.definitionFit: Salient means most noticeable or important, standing out, so it is a synonym of prominent.

clue.text: Make base answer with commoner behind enclosure

indicators.note: being behind means coming after, fixing which part goes first

blocks.note: ENC is the abbreviation for enclosure, as on a letter
A is the abbreviation for answer
an MP sits in the House of Commons

explanation.surface: Instructions for setting up a camp: respond alongside an ordinary person at the back of a pen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commoner' is not an ordinary person but a member of the House of Commons, the lower house of Britain's parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: To encamp is to set up a camp and settle there, establishing a base for troops or travellers.

clue.text: Bygone test is evocative of the country

blocks.note: bygone means past
an oral is a spoken exam

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned exam that brings rural life to mind.
explanation.walkthrough: An oral is a spoken examination, often part of a language exam.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastoral art or writing idealises rural life and shepherds, calling up images of countryside scenes.

clue.text: Chap that lifts

blocks.note: first meaning: a man's first name
second meaning: a crane for hoisting heavy loads

explanation.walkthrough: 'Chap' in crosswords often stands for any man's name; here the name is also a piece of lifting machinery.
explanation.definitionFit: Derrick is a common male forename, and a derrick is a crane or framework used for raising heavy weights.

clue.text: Unlucky nun pocketing nickel

indicators.note: to pocket something is to put it away inside, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: a nun is addressed as Sister
Ni is the chemical symbol for nickel

explanation.surface: A hapless nun slips a small coin into her habit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nickel' suggests the American five-cent coin, but it is the metal, contributing its chemical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinister originally meant left-handed and so inauspicious or ill-omened, the heraldic and archaic sense of unlucky.

clue.text: Go through support in front of church

indicators.note: being in front means placed first, fixing the running order

blocks.note: a pier is a supporting pillar
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A worshipper passes a pillar standing outside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: CE, for Church of England, is a common crossword abbreviation for church.
explanation.definitionFit: To pierce something is to make a hole right through it, so it is a synonym of penetrate.

clue.text: One who served review – critique ultimately managed

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: to vet something is to check or review it
the final letter of the word
to manage a business is to run it

explanation.surface: A former serviceman writes a review, and the critique finally gets done.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash splits the surface into two statements, but every word apart from the definition feeds the charade.
explanation.definitionFit: A veteran is someone who has served in the armed forces, especially over a long period.

clue.text: Require energy in spinning dive

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it
something spinning turns round, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: E is the symbol for energy
a dive is a seedy bar or den

explanation.surface: A diver needs strength to perform a twisting plunge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dive' reads as a plunge into water, but it is a disreputable drinking place.
explanation.definitionFit: To need something is to require it, so the two verbs are direct synonyms.

clue.text: Cheeky retriever running around lawn finally

indicators.note: running around is moving about all over the place, so the letters end up scattered
finally points to the end, so only the last letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: An impudent gun dog is dashing about the grass.
explanation.walkthrough: The dog and the lawn make a lively scene, but the dog's letters simply join the lawn's last letter and are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Irreverent means lacking proper respect, which fits cheeky in the sense of impudent or disrespectful.

clue.text: Lavish one left pondering

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner, someone who has left
pensive means deep in thought

explanation.surface: A generous person who has been abandoned sits thinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One left' reads as a single remaining item, but it is someone who walked out of a relationship.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lavish is rich and sumptuous, so it costs a great deal of money.

clue.text: Cheers from females taking in English painting, perhaps

indicators.note: taking something in means admitting it inside

blocks.note: hens are female birds, used loosely for women
E is the abbreviation for English
painting is an example of art

explanation.surface: Women applaud an English painting on show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheers' looks like a noun for applause, but it is a verb meaning encourages.
explanation.definitionFit: To hearten someone is to give them courage and hope, which is what cheering someone up does.

clue.text: Way Conservative, being embarrassed, gets trust

blocks.note: a street is a way or road
C is the abbreviation for Conservative
an embarrassed person goes red

explanation.surface: A very right-wing politician, despite blushing, earns people's confidence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Way Conservative' reads as slang for extremely conservative, but 'Way' is a road.
explanation.definitionFit: Street cred is credibility with ordinary or fashionable people, a kind of trust and standing among them.

clue.text: Bit of news, say, fixes up attack of the sulks

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, so backwards

blocks.note: to pin something is to fix it in place
a pet is a fit of sulking, as in 'in a pet'

explanation.surface: A news item, for instance, sets off a bout of bad temper.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'pet' in older British usage is a fit of pique; being 'in a pet' means sulking.
explanation.definitionFit: A snippet is a small piece of information, and a scrap of news is one example of that.

clue.text: Odyssey perhaps is some impressive picture

indicators.note: some of the following words means only a portion of them is used

blocks.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: Homer's Odyssey, say, paints an impressive picture.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is by example, flagged by 'perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Odyssey is a long heroic narrative poem, a classic example of the genre of heroic verse.

clue.text: I am up in box being a seller of drugs

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading bottom to top, so backwards
being in something means sitting inside it

blocks.note: I am contracts to I'm
a chest is a box

explanation.surface: A drug dealer confesses to being boxed in by the police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seller of drugs' suggests a dealer, but in Britain a chemist is a pharmacist or chemist's shop.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage a chemist is a pharmacist, who dispenses and sells medicines.

clue.text: Commercial diamonds head off outside

indicators.note: being outside means wrapping around, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: D is the card-suit abbreviation for diamonds
to head off trouble is to avert it

explanation.surface: A jewellery business heads out of the shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head off' could be a deletion signal, but here it is a phrasal verb meaning prevent.
explanation.definitionFit: A commercial is a television or radio advertisement, and advert is the British short form for one.

clue.text: Cover at home? Certainly

blocks.note: someone at home is in
sure is an informal yes, certainly

explanation.surface: An offer to shelter someone in the house, met with a keen yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover at home?' reads like home insurance, which makes the definition hide in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: To insure something is to arrange financial protection for it, which is what taking out cover means.

clue.text: Exorbitant starting price gathering support

indicators.note: to gather something is to take it in, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: SP is the betting abbreviation for starting price
a tee supports a golf ball

explanation.surface: An overpriced opening bid is winning backers.
explanation.walkthrough: SP is the starting price, the final odds on a horse when a race begins in British betting.
explanation.definitionFit: Steep is an informal word for prices that are unreasonably high, so it is a synonym of exorbitant.

clue.text: Get money from Fred finally twirling cane? It’s a performance

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the last letter is kept
twirling spins something round and round, so the letters come out mixed up

blocks.note: to tap someone is to ask them for money
the last letter of the name
taken as written

explanation.surface: Fred Astaire spinning his cane earns money on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: Fred Astaire, the Hollywood dancer famous for top hat and cane, sets the scene exactly.
explanation.definitionFit: Tap dancing is a stage routine of rhythmic steps, so a routine of it is one kind of show.

clue.text: Surplus old cleric turned up

indicators.note: in a down entry, turned up means flipped to read from bottom to top

blocks.note: Rev is short for Reverend, a cleric's title
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A surplus elderly priest appeared unexpectedly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned up' reads as arrived, but in a down clue it means read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Something over is left over, extra to what is needed, which is what surplus means.

clue.text: Maybe kipper is punter’s first order

indicators.note: first points to the start, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: the initial of the word
to order something in advance is to reserve it

explanation.surface: A smoked herring is a customer's opening choice in a café.
explanation.walkthrough: A kipper is a smoked, salted herring, a traditional British breakfast.
explanation.definitionFit: A kipper is fish that has been cured by smoking and salting, so it is one example of preserved food.

clue.text: Old Italian family? One objectively died here in France

blocks.note: me is the objective case of I, the word for oneself
D is the abbreviation for died
ici is French for here

explanation.surface: An ancient Italian dynasty, one of whose members died in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Objectively' is grammatical: I as the object of a verb becomes ME.
explanation.definitionFit: The Medici were a powerful banking dynasty who ruled Florence during the Renaissance.

clue.text: Head of Theology takes off to judge wall hanging?

indicators.note: the head is the top or start, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: the initial of the word
to take someone off is to mimic them, to ape them
a court tries a case, judging it

explanation.surface: A theology professor imitates others in order to evaluate a mural hanging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes off' reads as removing or departing, but in British usage it also means imitates for comic effect.
explanation.definitionFit: A tapestry is a woven textile with a picture on it, traditionally hung on castle walls.

clue.text: Declare a ton before international

indicators.note: coming before means placed in front, fixing the running order

blocks.note: taken as written
T is the abbreviation for ton
a Test is an international cricket match

explanation.surface: A batsman declares the innings after scoring a century in an international match.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket surface of a ton (a hundred runs) and declaring is misleading: the ton is just a weight abbreviation, and a Test is an international cricket match.
explanation.definitionFit: To attest is to state formally that something is true, giving evidence or bearing witness.
